name: Stainless steel bowls
why: Bowls make noise, nest inside each other, hold things and reflect light. A sitting baby can bang them, drop things in and tip them out, which is early cause and effect.
tip: Give 2–3 bowls of different sizes. Later they become drums, hats and sandpit buckets.

name: Wooden spoons
why: Easy to grip, safe to mouth and perfect for banging. Babies learn that their actions make sounds. Toddlers stir, drum and serve pretend food with them.
tip: Pair them with a steel bowl or a saucepan for a first drum kit.
safety: Check now and then for splinters. Untreated or oil-finished wood is best.

name: Balloon whisk
why: Light, shiny, springy and easy to hold. It's a classic treasure-basket object for babies exploring with hands and mouth.
tip: Push a soft fabric ball inside it and let the baby work out how to get it out.
safety: Choose a solid whisk whose wires are firmly fixed in the handle.

name: Treasure basket
why: Elinor Goldschmied's treasure basket is a low basket of everyday natural objects for a sitting baby to explore on their own: metal, wood, fabric, brush, leather. Babies concentrate on it for a surprisingly long time.
tip: A lovely gift: a basket with a wooden spoon, a whisk, a small steel bowl, a soft brush, a ring of keys from the hardware store and a scarf. Add a card that explains the idea.
safety: Every object should be bigger than a toilet-roll tube opening. Sit nearby, then let the baby lead.

name: Thin scarves for peekaboo
why: Peekaboo is the first game about things that disappear and come back (object permanence). The same scarves become capes, picnic blankets and dancing ribbons later.
tip: Look for light cotton or silk "play silks". Old scarves from a drawer work just as well.
safety: Supervised play only. Never leave fabric in the cot.

name: Tissue box of scarves to pull
why: Pulling things out of a hole is irresistible at this age. It trains the pincer grasp and gives a satisfying 'where did it go?' moment.
tip: Free to make: an empty tissue box with knotted scarves or cloth napkins inside.
safety: Remove the plastic film from the box opening.

name: Saucepan with a lid
why: Lids are a puzzle: on, off, clang. Babies figure out which lid fits, and toddlers use the pot for pretend cooking.
tip: Hand over an old pot from the cupboard. Ask the parents first if they have a spare.

name: Muffin tin + balls
why: One ball per hole is early one-to-one correspondence, the start of counting. Putting in and taking out is the main hobby of a 1-year-old.
tip: Pair a tin with tennis balls or soft fabric balls. Later, sort coloured socks into it.
safety: Balls must be larger than 4.5 cm.

name: Nesting measuring cups
why: They work as a stacking toy that's also a real kitchen tool: nesting, stacking, pouring and comparing sizes. Spatial skills like these predict later maths.
tip: Great for bath time and the sandpit too.

name: A big cardboard box
why: The joke that kids prefer the box is backed by research. Open-ended 'loose parts' invite more invention than single-purpose toys. A box becomes a cave, car, boat or rocket.
tip: Gift idea for older kids: a big box with a pack of crayons, tape and a note that says 'build anything'.
safety: Remove staples and plastic tape.

name: Tins with lids
why: Opening and closing lids, and hiding something inside to find later, builds fine motor control and memory. Toddlers will happily do it for ages.
tip: Old tea or biscuit tins are perfect. Put a surprise inside when you give them.
safety: Check the rims for sharp edges.

name: Colander + pipe cleaners
why: Poking pipe cleaners or straws through the holes is a focused fine motor 'posting' task that toddlers repeat over and over, practising the pincer grip they'll later use for pencils.
tip: Turn the colander upside down so the holes face up.
safety: Fold the sharp ends of pipe cleaners. Supervised play.

name: Pouring set: jug, funnel, cups
why: Water play in the bath or a washing-up bowl teaches volume, cause and effect, and hand control. It's also calming.
tip: Add a small sponge to squeeze.
safety: Always stay with a child near water.

name: Their own cup and cutlery
why: Drinking from an open cup and feeding themselves are CDC milestones toddlers are proud to reach. Real, child-size things invite them to try.
tip: Small stainless cutlery plus a small glass or steel cup.

name: Step stool for the kitchen counter
why: Pre-schoolers strongly prefer real activities to pretend ones and stay with them about twice as long. A stool lets them actually help: wash vegetables, stir, crack eggs.
tip: A gift parents use daily. A 'learning tower' is a safer, more expensive version for under-3s.
safety: Always supervise at the counter. Under 3 years, a learning tower with rails is safer.

name: Small broom and dustpan
why: Toddlers want to do what adults do. Real child-size tools make 'helping' possible and build independence and coordination.
tip: Get a real one, not a toy one: it actually works, and that's the point.

name: Small watering can
why: Watering plants is a real job with a visible result. It mixes gross motor skills (carrying) with care and patience.
tip: Add a pot of herb seeds for a complete gift.

name: Child-size garden tools
why: A real rake and spade that work let kids dig, sort leaves and help in the garden, which is real activity, outdoors and active.
tip: Metal heads with wooden handles last for years.

name: Big brushes for water painting
why: A bucket of water and a wide brush turns a fence or a wall into a canvas that dries and disappears. It's mess-free 'painting' that builds arm and hand control.
tip: Add a small bucket.

name: Sock-matching game
why: Pairing socks is real sorting and matching, the same skill memory games train, done while 'helping' with laundry.
tip: A gift twist: a pack of colourful kids' socks wrapped as a 'find the pairs' game.

name: Couch-cushion obstacle course
why: Crawling over, climbing on and jumping between cushions builds strength, balance and body awareness. The WHO recommends plenty of active play every day for this age.
tip: If you want to give a toy version: stackable floor cushions.
safety: Keep the course on a soft floor away from sharp furniture corners.

name: Paper roll + chunky crayons
why: Scribbling appears around 15–18 months and is the start of writing. A long roll on the floor gives room to make big arm movements.
tip: Tape the paper to the floor or the table.
safety: Choose chunky crayons for the youngest; they're harder to bite off and choke on.

name: Play dough
why: Squishing, rolling and cutting dough strengthens hand muscles needed later for writing, and it's endlessly open-ended.
tip: Homemade dough (flour, salt, water, oil) in a jar with a rolling pin and cookie cutters makes a cheap, lovely gift.
safety: Homemade dough is very salty; don't let it be eaten in quantity.

name: Ice-cube tray + tongs sorting
why: Moving pom-poms or beans into the cells with tongs trains the hand grip used for pencils, plus sorting and counting.
tip: Pair it with kitchen tongs or salad tongs from the drawer.
safety: Pom-poms and beans are choking hazards. Only for children who no longer mouth things, and supervised.

name: Sensory bin (rice, oats, lentils)
why: Scooping, pouring and hiding things in dry rice or oats is calming sensory play that also builds measuring and pretend play (a 'construction site', 'bakery').
tip: Gift a box with a lid, a scoop, a funnel and a few small toys to bury.
safety: Dry grains and lentils are a choking hazard under 3. Always supervise.

name: A real torch
why: Shadow puppets, den play and evening walks. Kids love a real tool that actually works rather than a toy copy.
tip: Pick one with a screw-closed battery compartment and normal AA/AAA batteries.
safety: Never coin/button batteries. The battery lid must need a screwdriver or be very hard to open.

name: Magnifying glass
why: In the 'real thing' study, a real microscope held kids' attention far longer than a toy one. A magnifier turns a walk into an expedition: bugs, leaves, snow crystals.
tip: Pair it with a jar for collecting (and releasing) bugs.

name: Wooden clothes pegs
why: Pinching a peg open is excellent pre-writing hand training. Clip them around a tin, sort them by colour, and use them to build a den with sheets.
tip: Add a cardboard ring with numbers to clip the matching number of pegs on.
safety: Pegs can pinch fingers, which is part of learning; the springs can come loose on cheap ones.

name: High-contrast baby book
why: Newborns see strong contrasts and faces best. A board book with bold black-and-white images is something to look at together during tummy time and while talking, and reading from birth is recommended by the AAP.
tip: Fold it open on the floor in front of a baby on their tummy.

name: Board books
why: Shared reading from early infancy predicts vocabulary and reading skills years later. Books also produced more back-and-forth talk than electronic toys in Sosa's study.
tip: Pick sturdy books with real photos of animals or everyday objects for the youngest. For older toddlers, books with rhymes and repetition.

name: Lift-the-flap books
why: Hidden things behind flaps combine reading with object permanence and fine motor practice. Toddlers ask for them again and again.
tip: Classics like 'Where's Spot?' (Hvor er Tassen?) never get old.

name: Picture books with a story
why: Stories build vocabulary, narrative skills and empathy. Talking about the pictures together is the 'dialogic reading' that boosts language most.
tip: Write a short dedication on the first page.

name: Baby-safe floor mirror
why: A mirror makes tummy time more interesting: babies lift their heads to look at the 'other baby'. Recognising themselves comes much later (around 18–24 months), which is fascinating to watch.
tip: Pick a shatterproof acrylic mirror made for babies.
safety: Never glass mirrors on the floor.

name: Wooden play gym
why: Hanging objects to look at, then swipe at, then grab follow the newborn-to-reaching milestones closely. A simple wooden frame is less overstimulating than flashing electronic gyms.
tip: Swap the hanging items now and then for new things to discover (a spoon, a soft ring).
safety: Remove once the baby can pull up on it.

name: Play mat for tummy time
why: At least 30 minutes of tummy time a day, spread out, is linked to earlier rolling, sitting and crawling. A soft mat with something to look at makes it more pleasant.
tip: A thick cotton blanket works fine. The mat mostly makes it a nice gift.

name: Simple mobile
why: Slow-moving shapes are good for the developing eyes of young babies, who track movement and contrast. It's a calm alternative to screens.
tip: Hang it above the changing table, where the baby spends lots of awake time.
safety: Remove from the cot once the baby can push up on hands and knees.

name: Soft rattle
why: Around 3–4 months babies start holding things, and a rattle rewards each shake with a sound. It's the first lesson in 'I can make things happen'.

name: Natural rubber teether
why: Everything goes in the mouth at this age. Mouthing is how babies explore. A natural rubber teether is easy to grasp and plastic-free.
safety: No amber teething necklaces (choking/strangulation risk). Check regularly for cracks.

name: Soft fabric ball
why: Grab, mouth, roll, chase, throw: a ball follows a child from reaching to running. Rolling it back and forth is also an early turn-taking game.

name: Object permanence box
why: Between 8 and 12 months babies start searching for hidden things. A box where the ball disappears and rolls back out is that discovery turned into a game.
tip: DIY: a shoebox with a hole cut in the lid and a tennis ball.

name: Stacking cups
why: First they're banged and mouthed, then nested, then stacked into towers, and later they're bath toys. Few toys last this long or teach size order this well.
tip: Plastic-free alternative: the steel bowls or measuring cups.

name: Pull-along toy
why: New walkers love having something follow them. It motivates walking and gives them a sense of control.
safety: Cords under 30 cm for under-3s.

name: Push walker
why: Pushing a stable walker lets a baby who is pulling up practise steps on their own terms. Later it becomes a cart for transporting treasures.
safety: Choose a push walker, never a sit-in baby walker (those are linked to injuries).

name: Wooden shape sorter
why: Fitting shapes into holes is spatial problem-solving: rotating, testing, trying again. Toddlers love to post things into holes anyway.
tip: Start with just one or two shapes, then add more.

name: Bead maze
why: Pushing beads along the wire builds hand-eye coordination and tracking, and the beads can't come off.

name: Wooden blocks
why: 3-year-olds who were better at copying block structures were better at early maths. Blocks are also the definition of open-ended, from knocking down to building whole cities.
tip: A plain set of unit blocks beats a themed set. Buy once, use for years.

name: Crane with blocks
why: Hoisting blocks combines building with mechanics: how a crank and rope work. It's good for building play together.

name: Duplo
why: Interlocking bricks are construction and spatial play that toddlers can actually manage. Durable, endlessly combinable, and good for a lifetime of resale.
tip: Secondhand Duplo is plentiful on FINN, so it's plastic without buying new plastic.

name: Knob puzzle
why: Puzzle play between ages 2 and 4 predicted better spatial skills at 4½ years, even after controlling for family income and parent talk. Knob puzzles are the entry point.
tip: Start with 3–5 pieces of familiar shapes or animals.

name: First jigsaw puzzles
why: Rotating pieces to fit is mental rotation, a spatial skill linked to later STEM. Solving puzzles together is also great talking time.
tip: 4–12 pieces at age 3, 20–50 by age 5.

name: Small steel pots and pans
why: Pretend cooking is the earliest role play (feeding a doll appears around 18 months). Steel versions look and sound real, which kids prefer.
tip: Combine with a few real kitchen items rather than buying a whole play kitchen.

name: Fabric play food
why: Naming, sorting and 'serving' food is language practice in disguise, and it supports the pretend play linked to social and language development.
tip: Real fruit in a basket works too, just not for long.

name: Doll or teddy with a bed
why: Caring for a doll (feeding, putting to bed) is how toddlers practise everyday routines and empathy. It's one of the CDC 18-month pretend milestones.

name: A cuddly soft toy
why: A comfort object helps many toddlers through transitions and sleep, and it becomes a main character in pretend play.
tip: Note: most soft toys are polyester (plastic). Look for organic cotton/wool if you want plastic-free.
safety: Keep soft toys out of the cot for babies under 1 year.

name: Hand and finger puppets
why: A puppet is a toy that only works when an adult talks, which is exactly the kind of interaction the AAP says matters most. Older kids use them to tell their own stories.

name: Wooden train set
why: Building a track is spatial planning, and driving the train is story play. All the major brands are compatible, so the set can grow over years and between friends.
tip: Start with a basic set. More track is always the best follow-up gift.
safety: Small connector parts in some sets; check the age label for under-3s.

name: Chunky toy vehicles
why: Pushing cars is an early pretend play and a great source of words (vroom, bus, stop!). Bigger, chunky vehicles are safe for small hands.

name: Play tunnel
why: Crawling through tunnels builds strength and coordination, and peekaboo at the other end is object permanence again.
tip: Plastic-free alternative: a row of open cardboard boxes.

name: Play tent
why: A hideaway of their own: a reading corner, house, shop or camp. A small space gives a child a sense of control and invites pretend play.
tip: Or gift a fitted sheet and clothes pegs for den-building.

name: Wooden balance board
why: Rocker, bridge, slide, car, bed: one curved board does dozens of jobs and builds balance and core strength. It's a perfect open-ended toy.
safety: Use on a rug or soft floor.

name: Pikler climbing triangle
why: Lets babies and toddlers practise pulling up, climbing and coming down safely at their own pace, which builds strength, risk assessment and confidence.
tip: A bigger group gift. Consider chipping in together.
safety: Put a soft mat underneath, and stay nearby when they first use it.

name: Balance bike
why: Kids learn balance first and usually skip training wheels later. It's daily exercise disguised as fun, in line with WHO's 3 hours of activity a day.
tip: A helmet is a great add-on gift.

name: Sand toys
why: Filling, pouring, building and baking cakes with sand is sensory, motor and pretend play rolled into one, outdoors.
tip: Plastic-free alternative: old metal spoons, a steel bowl and a muffin tin.

name: Simple instruments
why: Shakers, a drum or a xylophone make music a shared activity. Rhythm and singing together support language and turn-taking.
tip: Shakers for babies, a xylophone or drum from about 1 year.
safety: Homemade shakers must be sealed shut so nothing small falls out.

name: Easel with chalkboard
why: Drawing standing up uses the whole arm and shoulder, which is good pre-writing preparation, and a dedicated art spot invites daily drawing.
tip: Add the MÅLA paper roll on top of it.

name: A first cooperative board game
why: Taking turns, following rules and counting spaces are 3–4-year-old milestones. Cooperative games (everyone wins or loses together) are easier for little ones to handle.
tip: HABA 'First Orchard' (Min første frukthage) is a classic from age 2.

name: Picture domino
why: Matching pictures or dots and taking turns builds number sense and patience. It's quick enough for short attention spans.

name: Memory card game
why: Remembering where the match is trains working memory, and kids often beat the adults.
tip: Start with 6–8 pairs face up, then turn them over.

name: Magnetic building tiles
why: They make 3D building easy: flat shapes become cubes and towers. It's the same spatial assembly that predicts early maths.
safety: Only buy from reputable shops and throw away any cracked tile. Loose magnets are very dangerous if swallowed.

name: Dress-up box
why: Old hats, bags, scarves and jackets turn into characters. It's pretend play, storytelling and practice putting on clothes all at once.
tip: Collect from your own wardrobe or secondhand shops into a box. Skip the branded costumes.
safety: No cords or drawstrings around the neck.
